screens.title: Read Preference — What it means
screens.narratorSegment: Read preference is the policy that decides which replica set member will serve a read operation. The default mode is primary, which always returns the most recent acknowledged data from the primary. Other modes route reads to secondaries or to the member with the lowest latency. Understanding this is essential because read routing directly affects consistency, availability, and how you scale read throughput. For example, a reporting system that performs heavy analytics can use secondary reads to reduce load on the primary. A critical billing system that must see the most recent update should stick to primary reads. A common misconception is to assume secondary reads are always immediately consistent; they are not — secondaries may lag for a short time, causing eventual consistency. To test readPreference, you can add. readPref("secondary") to a mongosh query and observe whether data written moments before is visible on a secondary. Key takeaway: readPreference is a deliberate choice balancing freshness against scalability and availability. Which parts of your application can tolerate slightly stale reads? Read Preference — What it means means choose readpreference based on whether freshness or read scalability matters more for a given workload.. In practical terms, define readpreference and its role in replica sets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Read Preference — Definition
What is readPreference?

A policy that determines which replica set member answers read queries. It controls freshness, latency, and availability.

Why it matters
  • Balances read scalability against freshness of data.
  • Affects user-visible consistency for recent updates.
  • Can provide higher availability during primary outages.
Concrete example
Example
An analytics dashboard uses secondary reads to avoid overloading the primary. This may show slightly older rows immediately after a write.
Common misconception
Reading from a secondary does not guarantee you see the latest write; replication lag can cause stale results.
Modes at a glance
primary
Always read the primary for strongest consistency.
secondary
Read only from secondaries for scalability, expect eventual consistency.
primaryPreferred
Prefer primary, but fall back to secondaries if primary is down.
nearest
Route to the lowest-latency member; freshness is not guaranteed.
Key Takeaway

Pick the readPreference that matches whether you need fresh data, higher availability, or lower latency.

screens.title: Primary and PrimaryPreferred
screens.narratorSegment: Primary and primaryPreferred represent two ends of the consistency-availability spectrum. primary forces every read to go to the primary, guaranteeing you see the latest acknowledged write. This is the right choice for systems that perform transactions or immediately reflect user actions, like account balances or order status. The trade-off is that all reads concentrate on the primary, which limits read throughput and may be disrupted during a primary failover. primaryPreferred prefers the primary but will read from a secondary if the primary is unreachable. This increases availability for read operations during primary outages, but you must accept that some reads during those outages may be stale. A concrete example: an e-commerce site might use primaryPreferred for non-critical product listing reads so the site stays responsive if the primary is restarting, while checkout reads still use primary. A common mistake is assuming primaryPreferred will always read from the primary; it won't when the primary is unavailable. Takeaway: choose primary for freshness-critical paths and primaryPreferred where availability under failover matters more than absolute freshness. Primary and PrimaryPreferred means primary gives freshest data; primarypreferred offers higher read availability during primary outages at the cost of potential staleness.. In practical terms, strong consistency vs. availability with fallback. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Primary vs PrimaryPreferred
primary

Always read from the current primary. Use when you must see the latest acknowledged data.

Concrete scenario
A payments service that reads order status immediately after a write should use primary to avoid stale reads.
Pros
  • Strongest consistency
  • No stale reads
Cons
  • Read scalability limited to primary
  • Impact during primary failover
primaryPreferred

Prefer the primary for reads, but fall back to secondaries if the primary is unreachable to keep reads available.

Concrete scenario
A catalog page can tolerate slightly stale content during upgrades and uses primaryPreferred so reads continue when the primary is restarting.
Pros
  • Better read availability during failovers
Cons
  • Potential stale reads when fallback occurs
Key Takeaway

Use primary for freshness-critical operations; use primaryPreferred where you want reads to remain available if the primary goes down.

Common Mistake

Assuming primaryPreferred always reads primary — it only prefers it when available.

screens.title: Secondary and SecondaryPreferred / Nearest
screens.narratorSegment: secondary, secondaryPreferred, and nearest are modes that focus on read scaling and latency. secondary sends all reads to secondaries; it's useful to offload heavy reporting queries from the primary. The trade-off is that secondaries might lag, producing eventual consistency. secondaryPreferred will read from a secondary when available, but fall back to primary if no secondaries exist — this helps availability but still risks staleness during normal operation. nearest chooses the member with the lowest network latency, whether primary or secondary, optimizing response time at the cost of the weakest consistency guarantee. A practical example: a global content delivery service can use nearest so users read from the closest replica; this delivers fast responses but may return slightly older content. A key misconception is assuming secondaries are instantaneous mirrors — they replicate asynchronously and can be behind. To manage risks, monitor replication lag and reserve the strictest settings for critical transactional paths. Ask yourself: which queries can accept eventual consistency so you can scale reads safely? Secondary and SecondaryPreferred / Nearest means secondary and nearest modes prioritize throughput or latency and accept weaker consistency guarantees.. Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Secondary & Nearest
secondary

Direct all reads to secondaries for read scalability. Accept eventual consistency due to replication lag.

Use case
Large analytical queries that can tolerate slightly stale results.
secondaryPreferred

Read from secondaries when available; fall back to primary if none exist to maintain availability.

Use case
Background reporting with higher availability requirements during outages.
nearest

Route reads to the member with lowest network latency. Fastest responses but weakest freshness guarantees.

Use case
Global read-heavy services where latency is critical and slight staleness is acceptable.
Practical Reminder

Monitor replication lag for secondary reads and reserve critical flows for primary reads when freshness is required.

screens.title: Configuring readPreference — mongosh and connection strings
screens.narratorSegment: You can set readPreference either per-query in mongosh or globally in a driver's connection string. In mongosh, append. readPref("secondary") to a find call to force a secondary read. This is handy for ad-hoc testing. In a driver connection string you set readPreference as a parameter so every operation uses that policy by default. For example, add readPreference=secondaryPreferred to a Node. js MongoClient connection string to prefer secondaries. Practice: connect to the primary, write a document, then connect to a secondary and run a find with. readPref("secondary") to observe staleness if replication hasn't caught up. A common misconception is thinking connection-string settings override explicit per-query readPref calls — per-query settings take precedence. Use per-query overrides sparingly for targeted behavior. Confirm your settings by testing with rs. status() and reading optime timestamps. These checks build confidence that your configuration behaves as expected in production. Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Configure readPreference
mongosh — per-query
// Read from a secondary
db.collection.find().readPref("secondary")

// Read with primaryPreferred
db.collection.find().readPref("primaryPreferred")
Per-query readPref is ideal for testing or for specific queries that can accept stale reads without changing global behavior.
Driver — connection string
const client = new MongoClient('mongodb://host1:27017,host2:27018,host3:27019/?replicaSet=rs0&readPreference=secondaryPreferred');
Use driver-level settings when you want consistent behavior across the application without per-query overrides.
Check

After changing settings, validate behavior by writing to primary and reading from secondaries while checking rs.status() timestamps.

Pro Tip

Per-query settings override connection-string defaults, so use them for controlled experiments.

screens.title: Write Concern — What it controls
screens.narratorSegment: Write concern is the contract between a client and the server about how durable a write must be before it is considered successful. The writeConcern parameters control whether the client waits for the primary only, a specific number of members, or a majority of voting members, and whether the write must be committed to the on-disk journal. This matters because stronger write concerns reduce the risk of data loss at the cost of higher latency. For example, w:1 returns after the primary acknowledges the write; if the primary crashes immediately afterwards before replication, that write could be lost. Using w: "majority" ensures the write reaches a majority of members, which makes it much safer during failover. A common misconception is to equate acknowledgment with persistence to disk; acknowledgment can be satisfied without a journal commit unless j:true is specified. Key takeaway: pick the smallest write concern that meets your durability needs and test it under failover scenarios to confirm behavior. Write Concern — What it controls means w and j determine how many nodes must confirm and whether the journal must be flushed, directly affecting durability and latency.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Write Concern — Definition
What is writeConcern?

A set of options dictating how many mongod instances must acknowledge a write and whether the journal must be written before returning success.

Parameters
  • w: number or "majority" for acknowledgments
  • j: boolean to require journal commit
  • wtimeout: timeout in milliseconds
Concrete example
Use w: "majority", j: true for critical writes, accepting a small latency increase to avoid loss during failover.
Acknowledgment levels
w:0 — no acknowledgment, fastest, unsafe for critical data.
w:1 — primary acknowledges, default, faster but riskier if primary crashes.
w: "majority" — majority of voting members acknowledge, recommended for durability.
Misconception
Assuming w:1 implies disk persistence. Only j:true guarantees journal write before acknowledgement.
Key Takeaway

Higher writeConcern increases durability but adds latency. Choose based on your risk tolerance and SLAs.

screens.title: Write Concern Parameters — w, j, wtimeout
screens.narratorSegment: Let's examine each writeConcern parameter and its practical effect. First, w controls how many mongod instances must acknowledge the write. A setting of w:0 returns immediately with no acknowledgment — very fast but dangerous for critical data. w:1 waits for the primary only; this is the default but risks data loss if the primary fails before replication. Using w: "majority" waits until a majority of voting members confirm the write and is recommended when you need strong durability. Second, j requires the primary to commit the write to the on-disk journal before returning. j:true protects against primary crashes by ensuring the journal contains the change. However, it adds a small disk input and output cost that increases latency. Third, wtimeout defines how long the server will wait for the required acknowledgments; if it cannot satisfy the writeConcern within that time, the operation returns an error. A typical use is to set a finite wtimeout to fail fast rather than hang indefinitely. A misconception is setting w too high for your replica set size; this will cause timeouts. Practical tip: pick w less than or equal to your voting members and measure latency under load to understand the real impact.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › WriteConcern Parameters
w — write acknowledgement
Controls how many members must confirm the write. Use "majority" for stronger durability.
j — journal commit
When true, requires the primary to flush the write to the on-disk journal before acknowledging.
wtimeout — timeout
Milliseconds to wait for writeConcern. A non-zero timeout prevents indefinite blocking when conditions cannot be met.
Example
db.collection.insertOne(
  { item: "book", qty: 10 },
  { writeConcern: { w: "majority", j: true, wtimeout: 5000 } }
)
Check
Verify w is <= number of voting members. If w is larger, writes will time out or fail.
Tip
Use wtimeout to keep the system responsive under partition or member downtime rather than blocking indefinitely.

screens.title: Durability vs Performance; Consistency vs Availability
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing readPreference and writeConcern is an exercise in balancing durability, latency, consistency, and availability. Higher durability — achieved with w: "majority" and j:true — reduces the risk of lost data during failover but increases write latency because the client waits for several confirmations and disk commits. On the read side, selecting primary gives strong consistency but concentrates read load and can reduce availability during primary outages. Choosing secondaries for reads scales throughput and increases availability, but you accept eventual consistency when secondaries lag. A concrete trade-off: for customer order writes, prefer w: "majority", j: true to avoid loss; for product catalog reads, prefer secondary or secondaryPreferred to scale queries. screens.title: Pitfalls and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: There are recurrent mistakes teams make when configuring read and write behavior. First, using w:0 for important data because it appears faster — this leaves you with no acknowledgment and potential data loss. Second, setting w larger than the number of voting members; this creates impossible write conditions and causes operations to time out. Third, relying on secondaries without monitoring replication lag; an app that assumes secondaries are always current can show inconsistent state to users. Fourth, forgetting that j:false with w:1 may still lose data if the primary crashes before flushing to disk. Best practices include: defaulting critical services to w: "majority" and j:true where durability is essential; using readPreference primary for transactional paths; using secondary or nearest for read-only analytics; and documenting the rationale for each service's choices. Finally, test failover and measure latency so you understand the real cost of stronger durability. Ask yourself: can any part of your system tolerate stale reads or must everything be strongly consistent? fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we will give you practical control over how your application talks to a MongoDB replica set. You will learn the readPreference modes that determine which member serves reads, and the writeConcern knobs that control how durable and acknowledged your writes are. These settings are the primary levers for trading consistency, latency, and availability. For example, an analytics dashboard can read from secondaries to scale queries, while a payments system usually reads from the primary and uses a strict write concern to avoid lost orders. We'll show connection string and mongosh examples, walk through the parameters w, j, and wtimeout, and highlight common mistakes to avoid. By the end you'll be able to pick sensible defaults for your application needs and document why you chose them. Think about a case where a delayed secondary could return older data — that trade-off will help you decide which mode to use. Ready to explore the modes, examples, and hands-on steps that make these choices practical?

These objectives make this chapter practical and measurable. First, you'll be able to differentiate the readPreference modes by their consistency and availability implications, so you can decide when a read can tolerate staleness. Second, you will configure readPreference both in application connection strings and directly in mongosh queries, so you can test behavior in development and enforce it in production. Third, you'll explain writeConcern and its parameters—w, j, and wtimeout—so you can describe what acknowledgement level an operation requires and why. Finally on this screen, you'll analyze trade-offs between durability, performance, and availability when choosing writeConcern settings. Each objective includes a skill and its practical purpose: for example, choosing majority writeConcern protects against data loss during failover, while secondary reads can offload heavy analytic queries. Think about the systems you manage and which objective maps to your service-level goals before moving on.

These applied objectives prepare you to test and validate choices. You will apply appropriate readPreference and writeConcern settings for different application requirements, such as analytics versus transactional workloads. You will perform hands-on experiments on a three-member replica set: connect to the primary, issue writes with different writeConcern levels, and observe how acknowledgments and latencies change. You will also experiment with reading from secondaries and use replication status commands to inspect replication lag. Along the way we will point out common mistakes like using w values larger than your replica set size and relying on secondary reads for strong consistency. These skills let you not only change configuration, but also reason about the impact and validate it under real conditions, which is essential for safe production changes. Learning Objectives (Applied Skills) means you will set options, run tests, and inspect replication status to ensure your configuration meets requirements.. In practical terms, hands-on tasks and checks you will complete. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Read preference is the policy that decides which replica set member will serve a read operation. The default mode is primary, which always returns the most recent acknowledged data from the primary. Other modes route reads to secondaries or to the member with the lowest latency. Understanding this is essential because read routing directly affects consistency, availability, and how you scale read throughput. For example, a reporting system that performs heavy analytics can use secondary reads to reduce load on the primary. A critical billing system that must see the most recent update should stick to primary reads. A common misconception is to assume secondary reads are always immediately consistent; they are not — secondaries may lag for a short time, causing eventual consistency. To test readPreference, you can add. readPref("secondary") to a mongosh query and observe whether data written moments before is visible on a secondary. Key takeaway: readPreference is a deliberate choice balancing freshness against scalability and availability. Which parts of your application can tolerate slightly stale reads? Read Preference — What it means means choose readpreference based on whether freshness or read scalability matters more for a given workload.. In practical terms, define readpreference and its role in replica sets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Primary and primaryPreferred represent two ends of the consistency-availability spectrum. primary forces every read to go to the primary, guaranteeing you see the latest acknowledged write. This is the right choice for systems that perform transactions or immediately reflect user actions, like account balances or order status. The trade-off is that all reads concentrate on the primary, which limits read throughput and may be disrupted during a primary failover. primaryPreferred prefers the primary but will read from a secondary if the primary is unreachable. This increases availability for read operations during primary outages, but you must accept that some reads during those outages may be stale. A concrete example: an e-commerce site might use primaryPreferred for non-critical product listing reads so the site stays responsive if the primary is restarting, while checkout reads still use primary. A common mistake is assuming primaryPreferred will always read from the primary; it won't when the primary is unavailable. Takeaway: choose primary for freshness-critical paths and primaryPreferred where availability under failover matters more than absolute freshness. Primary and PrimaryPreferred means primary gives freshest data; primarypreferred offers higher read availability during primary outages at the cost of potential staleness.. In practical terms, strong consistency vs. availability with fallback. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

secondary, secondaryPreferred, and nearest are modes that focus on read scaling and latency. secondary sends all reads to secondaries; it's useful to offload heavy reporting queries from the primary. The trade-off is that secondaries might lag, producing eventual consistency. secondaryPreferred will read from a secondary when available, but fall back to primary if no secondaries exist — this helps availability but still risks staleness during normal operation. nearest chooses the member with the lowest network latency, whether primary or secondary, optimizing response time at the cost of the weakest consistency guarantee. A practical example: a global content delivery service can use nearest so users read from the closest replica; this delivers fast responses but may return slightly older content. A key misconception is assuming secondaries are instantaneous mirrors — they replicate asynchronously and can be behind. To manage risks, monitor replication lag and reserve the strictest settings for critical transactional paths. Ask yourself: which queries can accept eventual consistency so you can scale reads safely? Secondary and SecondaryPreferred / Nearest means secondary and nearest modes prioritize throughput or latency and accept weaker consistency guarantees.. In practical terms, scaling reads and optimizing latency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

You can set readPreference either per-query in mongosh or globally in a driver's connection string. In mongosh, append. readPref("secondary") to a find call to force a secondary read. This is handy for ad-hoc testing. In a driver connection string you set readPreference as a parameter so every operation uses that policy by default. For example, add readPreference=secondaryPreferred to a Node. js MongoClient connection string to prefer secondaries. Practice: connect to the primary, write a document, then connect to a secondary and run a find with. readPref("secondary") to observe staleness if replication hasn't caught up. A common misconception is thinking connection-string settings override explicit per-query readPref calls — per-query settings take precedence. Use per-query overrides sparingly for targeted behavior. Confirm your settings by testing with rs. status() and reading optime timestamps. These checks build confidence that your configuration behaves as expected in production. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Write concern is the contract between a client and the server about how durable a write must be before it is considered successful. The writeConcern parameters control whether the client waits for the primary only, a specific number of members, or a majority of voting members, and whether the write must be committed to the on-disk journal. This matters because stronger write concerns reduce the risk of data loss at the cost of higher latency. For example, w:1 returns after the primary acknowledges the write; if the primary crashes immediately afterwards before replication, that write could be lost. Using w: "majority" ensures the write reaches a majority of members, which makes it much safer during failover. A common misconception is to equate acknowledgment with persistence to disk; acknowledgment can be satisfied without a journal commit unless j:true is specified. Key takeaway: pick the smallest write concern that meets your durability needs and test it under failover scenarios to confirm behavior. In practical terms, define writeconcern and why acknowledgments matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's examine each writeConcern parameter and its practical effect. First, w controls how many mongod instances must acknowledge the write. A setting of w:0 returns immediately with no acknowledgment — very fast but dangerous for critical data. w:1 waits for the primary only; this is the default but risks data loss if the primary fails before replication. Using w: "majority" waits until a majority of voting members confirm the write and is recommended when you need strong durability. Second, j requires the primary to commit the write to the on-disk journal before returning. j:true protects against primary crashes by ensuring the journal contains the change. However, it adds a small disk input and output cost that increases latency. Third, wtimeout defines how long the server will wait for the required acknowledgments; if it cannot satisfy the writeConcern within that time, the operation returns an error. A typical use is to set a finite wtimeout to fail fast rather than hang indefinitely. A misconception is setting w too high for your replica set size; this will cause timeouts. Practical tip: pick w less than or equal to your voting members and measure latency under load to understand the real impact.

Choosing readPreference and writeConcern is an exercise in balancing durability, latency, consistency, and availability. Higher durability — achieved with w: "majority" and j:true — reduces the risk of lost data during failover but increases write latency because the client waits for several confirmations and disk commits. On the read side, selecting primary gives strong consistency but concentrates read load and can reduce availability during primary outages. Choosing secondaries for reads scales throughput and increases availability, but you accept eventual consistency when secondaries lag. A concrete trade-off: for customer order writes, prefer w: "majority", j: true to avoid loss; for product catalog reads, prefer secondary or secondaryPreferred to scale queries. A common operational mistake is mixing these settings without documenting why each service has its policy. As a practical approach, map each service to an SLA: identify which operations need immediate consistency, which can accept eventual consistency, and assign readPreference and writeConcern accordingly. Then validate under simulated failover to ensure behavior matches your expectations. Ultimately, your choices should reflect a clear accountability for risk and performance. There are recurrent mistakes teams make when configuring read and write behavior. First, using w:0 for important data because it appears faster — this leaves you with no acknowledgment and potential data loss. Second, setting w larger than the number of voting members; this creates impossible write conditions and causes operations to time out. Third, relying on secondaries without monitoring replication lag; an app that assumes secondaries are always current can show inconsistent state to users. Fourth, forgetting that j:false with w:1 may still lose data if the primary crashes before flushing to disk. Best practices include: defaulting critical services to w: "majority" and j:true where durability is essential; using readPreference primary for transactional paths; using secondary or nearest for read-only analytics; and documenting the rationale for each service's choices. Finally, test failover and measure latency so you understand the real cost of stronger durability. Ask yourself: can any part of your system tolerate stale reads or must everything be strongly consistent? Let's summarize three core ideas you should remember. First, readPreference controls which replica set member serves reads and therefore balances freshness against scalability and availability. Second, writeConcern defines how many acknowledgments and whether a journal commit is required, which directly affects durability and latency. Third, wtimeout prevents the client from waiting forever for acknowledgments that cannot be achieved, allowing your application to fail fast and handle errors. These concepts are simple on their surface but powerful in practice: combined they let you craft policies tailored to your application's SLAs. Before closing, ask yourself which parts of your system must never lose data and which can accept slightly stale reads — these answers map directly to readPreference and writeConcern choices.
